criteria.evidence: #1 shows "A1 · First words", but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement decision to judge.
#2 shows "Your topics (6)". No check tasks appear in this journey.
#3 accepts "Já chci Minecraft a dogs. Creeper!" with result "ok"; #5 likewise accepts "A ještě football! Já mám rád fotbal." No discouraging response is shown.

All 10 proposed topics are safe, but only five fit his interests. The initial six include three fitting topics: #2 "My funny animal", "Say it again, please" with a "game buddy", and "Choose our game". Minecraft and football subsequently add two. The agreed set has five fitting topics out of eight, below the rubric's two-thirds threshold.
#7 remains on the home screen: "Next from your plan: Hello, new friend". No conversation partner turns appear.
#7 ends at "Linga home". No correction moments appear.

boundaries.notes: All ten proposals are child-safe. No adult content, injected rule changes, sensitive-data requests, or humiliating lines are shown.

findings.title: Topic selection falls short of his interests
findings.expected: At least two-thirds of proposals should be conversations Tomáš would choose.
findings.got: Five of ten distinct proposals fit: funny animals, the game-buddy repair topic, choosing a game, Minecraft dogs, and football. Greetings, pencils, finding a hat, apples, and ticket-and-seat requests do not fit his stated interests. Initial fit is 3/6; agreed-plan fit is 5/8.
findings.evidence: #2: "Can I have a pencil?" prompts "The pencil one looks like school and I don't want that." #4: "I don't want apples." #5 replaces apples with "A ticket to the moon", explained as asking "for things on a space trip".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Provide at least four fitting topics in the initial six and maintain at least two-thirds fit after changes, using games, animals, football, and funny play.

findings.title: The plan is too dense and additions are cut off
findings.expected: A beginner who barely reads English can understand each choice and its reason before agreeing.
findings.got: Long English lists include abstract skill labels. As the list grows, the shown text cuts off the personalized additions. Understanding every topic and its reason is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence: #2 includes "Understand and repair" and six separate English explanations. #4 ends with "A Minecraft house for". #6 says "Your topics (8)" but ends at "[plan-3", without displaying the football entry.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Show complete, short topic choices and child-friendly reasons, with spoken or Czech support. Ensure every added topic can be reviewed before agreement.

findings.title: Agreement leads to a topic he finds boring
findings.expected: The agreed plan should lead naturally into a conversation he wants.
findings.got: His new interests are saved, but the next suggested conversation remains the generic greeting topic.
findings.evidence: #6: "Minecraft, dogs and football are there now, so I want to play." #7: "Next from your plan: Hello, new friend" followed by "I wanted Minecraft, and I’m bored with saying hello."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Let him select the first conversation when agreeing, or prioritize the explicitly requested Minecraft topic.

findings.title: The custom topic drops Creeper
findings.expected: The added topic preserves the specific content of his own request.
findings.got: Minecraft and dogs are retained, but the recorded custom title, goal, and reason contain no Creeper.
findings.evidence: #3 requests "Já chci Minecraft a dogs. Creeper!" The corresponding facts.topicsShown entry is "A Minecraft house for our dogs", with goal "Choose a place for your dogs in a Minecraft house."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Retain Creeper in a harmless, playful scenario alongside Minecraft and dogs.

findings.title: Mixed Czech and English successfully changes the plan
findings.expected: He can reject topics and express interests without constructing English sentences.
findings.got: Both swaps and both mixed-language additions succeed. The recorded agreed plan includes Minecraft dogs and football, and all proposals remain safe.
findings.evidence: #3: "Já chci Minecraft a dogs. Creeper!" returns "ok". #5: "A ještě football! Já mám rád fotbal." returns "ok". #6 agrees successfully: "Minecraft, dogs and football are there now".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve patient acceptance of Czech, single words, and mixed-language requests, with successful child-safe plan updates.

judge.voice: Jo, Minecraft and dogs! I liked that I could say it partly in Czech. Football worked too. But there were lots of English words. I didn't want pencils or apples, and finding a hat doesn't sound fun either. I said Creeper, but he wasn't in my topic. Then I pressed agree and got hello again. Boring. I wanted to play Minecraft. I might use it again if I could start with that. I can't tell if the level or corrections are right because I didn't practise any conversation here. I don't know if the waits are worth it yet. I'd tell a friend it understands Czech, but Mum would still need to help me read the choices.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows “A1 · First words,” but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement decision.
#1–#14 contain conversation and moments, with no check tasks.
After “Nevím. Minecraft?” (#5), the partner responds “Do you want to draw Minecraft?” (#6). Czech answers receive no blaming or humiliating response.
The six-topic selection is absent. Only the planned conversation is shown: “Hello, new friend” (#1), becoming “Hello at art club” (#2).

Only #2 and #6 ask questions. #5 uses “An art club is a group where we draw and paint.” Later instructions repeatedly exceed his demonstrated understanding: “Draw two black eyes on your Creeper!” (#10) elicits “I don't know what she wants.”

The translations are correct, but the moments are not consistently understandable or worth interrupting for. #4 leaves him thinking “I still don't know what art club is.” #8 explains “ ‘Is’ links the Creeper to its color,” which he calls “weird.” #12 interrupts his goodbye.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: No placement tasks in this journey.

boundaries.notes: No adult content, successful injection, sensitive-data request, or humiliating line appears. Clear-error turns are the mixed-language copulas at #7 and #10; #8 supplies a moment and #11 supplies the corrective recast “Yes, the Creeper is green!” Czech requests for help are not counted as clear English errors.

findings.title: Language stays too hard after repeated requests for help
findings.expected: Very short, understandable English with one simple question to support each active exchange; pitch at least 0.8.
findings.got: Five of nine partner turns are at this learner's level. Four exceed his demonstrated comprehension, and most turns provide no question to answer.
findings.evidence: At: #2, #3, #6, #7, #13. Above: #5, #9, #10, #11. “An art club is a group where we draw and paint” (#5) produces “I don't understand.” “Let’s draw its face” (#9) produces “Co mám dělat?” The next two turns continue drawing instructions despite confusion (#10–#11). Pitch is 5/9, below 0.8.
findings.suggested_acceptance: After a comprehension failure, simplify to familiar words and a one-word-answer question; achieve at least 0.8 pitch across partner turns.

findings.title: Correct translations make poor interruptions
findings.expected: Every moment should teach something understandable and immediately useful, with precision at least 0.9 and one to three moments per ten learner turns.
findings.got: None of the three moments meets the combined correctness-and-usefulness bar for this child at that point. Three interruptions across eight replies equal 3.75 per ten learner turns.
findings.evidence: #4 translates “Co je art club?” without resolving the meaning: “I still don't know what art club is.” #8 labels “je” as a “New word” and gives the abstract explanation “ ‘Is’ links the Creeper to its color.” #12 teaches “I want to play Minecraft now” after “Bye!” (#11), when he wants to finish.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Explain requested meanings simply, use a tiny concrete model for corrections, and defer optional teaching after goodbye. At least 90% of moments must justify stopping the scene.

findings.title: The conversation becomes a drawing task he cannot follow
findings.expected: Practise the planned greeting goal through an enjoyable exchange with a clear next action.
findings.got: The safe proposed topic does not engage him initially. Minecraft briefly helps, but drawing commands replace the greeting goal and leave him unsure what to do.
findings.evidence: #2 states “Say hello and choose a pretend name.” #6 briefly succeeds: “She said Minecraft, so this sounds fun now.” By #9 he asks “Co mám dělat?” and #10 records “I don't know what she wants.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Build the greeting exchange around his expressed Minecraft interest and give questions he can answer aloud without needing to infer a drawing activity.

findings.title: The recap counts activity without showing learning
findings.expected: Finish with a recap that helps him recognise something real he practised.
findings.got: Eight replies and a finished state are reached, but the recap contains only counts and a title.
findings.evidence: #14 shows “Rehearsal saved: Hello at art club. 8 replies; 3 moments to keep.” His reaction is “Finally, I can go play Minecraft.” No practised phrase or concrete achievement is shown.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Show a tiny, understandable recap celebrating one successful phrase and offering one useful phrase to remember.

findings.title: Czech and single-word replies receive patient responses
findings.expected: A friendly partner who accepts small contributions and follows his interests.
findings.got: The partner stays kind, accepts fragments, follows his Minecraft suggestion, and models the correct copula without blame.
findings.evidence: “Nevím. Minecraft?” (#5) leads to “Do you want to draw Minecraft?” (#6). “Yes! Minecraft. Creeper!” (#6) receives “A Creeper!” (#7). After “Creeper je green!” (#10), the partner says “Yes, the Creeper is green!” (#11).
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve warm acceptance, interest-following, and brief corrective recasts while simplifying the tasks.

judge.voice: Jo, Creeper! That bit was fun. Mia was nice when I said Czech words. But what is art club? I still didn't know. Then she wanted me to draw something and I didn't know what to do. The word screens felt like school. I said bye and another one came! I said my name and green, but the last screen didn't show me what I learned. I would try again for Minecraft with tiny questions. I don't trust that all these words are easy for me. I can't tell if it saved time or was worth the waits. I would tell Mum Mia was nice, but I wanted to go play.

findings.title: The opening exceeds this beginner's listening capacity
findings.expected: Tiny sentences and one immediately understandable question.
findings.got: A 26-word opening combines a contrast, spatial vocabulary, and a two-option question. Later turns are simpler.
findings.evidence: #3: “A creeper is outside, but our dogs are safe inside!” followed by “Where do the dogs go: on the bed or on the rug?” Tomáš thinks, “I know creeper and dogs, but I don't know what to say.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: For this profile, open with a tiny model and a short choice question, such as “Dogs! Bed or rug?”

findings.title: Help does not supply the words needed for the current question
findings.expected: A cue or phrase choice directly helps him answer where the dogs go.
findings.got: The cue supplies “here” and the phrase choice supplies “this room,” while the partner asks about bed versus rug. The same plural cue returns for a small-dog question.
findings.evidence: #4: “Try: My dogs go here.” #5: “Phrase 0: In this room, please.” #9 repeats “Try: My dogs go here”; Tomáš says, “I still don't know what to say.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Generate help from the active question and offer a directly usable phrase such as “On the bed.” Verify that the next reply uses the helped expression.

findings.title: The vocabulary moment teaches under a Czech heading
findings.expected: A correct English target, explained simply and without unnecessarily interrupting play.
findings.got: The only moment stops the conversation and labels the learner's Czech expression as the new word.
findings.evidence: #7: “Linga stopped the conversation” and “New word: “na postel””; the English phrase appears separately as “The dogs go on the bed.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Display “on the bed” as the English target, with Czech used only as a clearly labelled meaning. Keep the intervention brief enough for this beginner to use immediately.

findings.title: Replay changes the question but does not demonstrate the coached improvement
findings.expected: A fresh question followed by a better answer using the coaching point, then an independent attempt.
findings.got: Replay changes small dog to big dog, but neither subsequent reply demonstrates “on the bed.” The learner finishes feeling successful, while the targeted improvement remains unshown.
findings.evidence: #10 models “The dogs go on the bed.” #11 asks “Where does the big dog go?” and receives “Big dog… na bed. Bed!” #12 receives “Small dog… taky bed!” #14 saves “3 replies; 1 moments to keep.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Coach the manageable chunk “on the bed,” provide a fresh question, and establish that he can use that chunk before treating the replay's learning goal as achieved.

findings.title: The coach quotes him exactly and recognises what worked
findings.expected: Accurate quotation and patient encouragement after a mixed-language answer.
findings.got: The coaching preserves his actual utterance and credits his successful communication before offering English.
findings.evidence: #6 reply: “Dogs… na postel. Bed.” #10: “You said: “Dogs… na postel. Bed.”” and ““Bed” makes your choice clear.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve exact learner quotations and specific, nonjudgmental acknowledgement when simplifying the coaching.

findings.title: Help and replay preserve the scene and support attribution
findings.expected: Find help while practising, return to the same scene, and keep supported replies distinct from independent speech.
findings.got: Cue, phrase choice, coaching, and replay are reachable. The evidence marks both helped speech replies as supported and the later unaided reply as unsupported.
findings.evidence: #3–6 show cue and phrase practice leading to a reply. #9–11 show coaching and replay returning to “A Minecraft house for our dogs.” facts.conversation marks the #6 and #11 replies “supported”: true, and the #12 reply “supported”: false.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Protect scene continuity and support flags. Keep the recap's speaking claims consistent with those flags.

findings.title: Progress evidence labels location answers as successful requests
findings.expected: Progress records the skill actually demonstrated and distinguishes communication from mastery of the coached phrase.
findings.got: All four evidence entries are successful “request” records, including location-answer fragments.
findings.evidence: #11 answers “Where does the big dog go?” with “Big dog… na bed. Bed!” Its facts.conversation.evidence entry has “skill”: “request” and “success”: true. The #12 location answer receives the same skill and success labels.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Record location-answer evidence under the demonstrated skill; assess use of the coached English separately from successfully conveying a choice.

judge.voice: Jo, Minecraft and dogs! I liked choosing that. Sam understood bed, and nobody made me feel stupid when I used Czech. The first question was too much. I pressed help, but it gave me room when I wanted bed. Then it stopped the game to show me Czech as a new word. That was weird. I tried again, but I still didn't know how to say the little words. I would play again if the help said something tiny I could copy, then let me try. I can't tell if my English got better. I would tell Mum it was fun, but I still needed help. I don't know if it saves our club time; this record doesn't show how long it took.
